Answer B is accurate and covers everything too, but it mostly asks for recited rules and numbers, includes weak filler options like 'It doesn't matter' and 'Fix it yourself', and gives almost no explanation. pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Answer B sets every question on the warehouse floor, uses wrong options a new hire might actually pick, and explains each one. It covers every topic in the session. pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Answer A turns every topic into a warehouse-floor scenario, uses believable wrong options, and explains why the right answer is right and why each tempting wrong one fails. samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers explain the failures well and tie each rewrite to the actual submission. A's rewrite for the missing-customers query is the better teaching comment: it has the student compare row counts and work out which join type keeps unmatched rows. B just tells the student to use a LEFT JOIN. B's rewrites are tighter and closer to what a TA would really write, but A's lead on the most important teaching point outweighs its extra length. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers explain clearly why the original comments fail. Both also catch that "needs improvement on joins" is factually wrong. B's rewrite for the missing-customers query teaches better: it has the student compare row counts and work out the join type themselves. But B's rewrites are long, with bullets, office-hours invitations and career asides, so few TAs would actually leave them. A's rewrites are concise, respectful and specific, though A states the LEFT JOIN fix outright and leaves an awkward bracketed placeholder in rewrite #2.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers diagnose the originals well and write specific, respectful rewrites. A edges ahead: its zero-order rewrite ends with a question, so the student works out the COUNT/NULL issue themselves, and its comments are slightly tighter. B adds a detail the submission never mentioned (the subquery 'pull[s] in the customer data') and gives away the COUNT(*) fix outright. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers diagnose the original comments well and give rewrites with similar structure. B's rewrite for the missing-customers query does more to lead the student to the cause, ending with a question about COUNT and NULLs, while A walks through the fix more directly. A also adds an unsupported detail (the subquery 'pulls in customer data'), and B has small inventions of its own ('b.id', a column named 'count'). Both rewrites for the slow query ask for two changes rather than one, and both are a bit long for a typical TA comment.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers diagnose the originals well and rewrite all three comments in nearly the same way. B's critique is slightly sharper on the unexplained score and the factual error in comment 3. However, B's rewrite 2 says the student's 'counting logic is right', which the submission never established and which clashes with B's own COUNT(*) warning. A stays closer to the submissions and gives a concrete self-check: compare the result's row count with the customers count, or use EXPLAIN. Both rewrites for the slow query name two changes rather than one, and both are a little long for a typical TA comment. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): The two answers are very close in structure and substance. B edges ahead on rewrite 2: it adds a concrete self-check (compare the result's row count against COUNT(*) FROM customers), and it avoids A's unsupported claim that the student's counting logic was right. Both rewrites for the slow query name two changes rather than one, and both hand over the LEFT JOIN fix instead of letting the student find it, so neither scores top marks on items 3 and 4.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers say plainly that the current numbers are not enough, and both give the director honest wording. samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Answer A teaches the three untouched units first. During those weeks, calculations comes back every Friday, and drug classes and law alternate on Saturdays. From Week 5 it mixes all six units together, and every review is active recall plus an error log, with no invented exam details. Answer B covers the new units and then reviews each old unit in its own block. Law disappears until Week 7, and topics barely recur, though B's single week-by-week table is easier to read on a fridge. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B keeps all three previously studied units in the plan from week 1: calculations every Friday, with drug classes and law alternating on Saturdays. It then moves to interleaved mixed practice and builds active recall into every session. A drops drug classes and law entirely for weeks 1–4 and then reviews each in its own block, which weakens spaced review, though its day-level topic detail is useful. pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A fits everything on one week-by-day grid. It brings the earlier units back on Saturdays and in mixed recall, keeps answering from memory central, and uses placeholders for exam details it doesn't know. B also stays within the time limits and teaches the new units first, but its phase templates are harder to read at a glance on a fridge. It also relies more on rereading and skimming, and it assumes 60- and 90-question tests without flagging that as a guess. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B is the better fridge schedule for this request. It builds the plan around answering from memory, using blank-paper recall, an error log and new practice questions instead of rereading. It uses placeholders instead of guessing exam length or passing score, and puts everything in one week-by-day grid. B's mistakes are that it adds a partial 'Start' week and its dates don't agree: it assumes the exam is on Thursday 17 Dec, but the grid places it on Saturday. A is clear and keeps calculations and drug classes coming back every week, but it relies more on 'review notes' and 'skim'. pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B keeps all three previously studied units in daily closed-book recall from week 1 and uses mixed question sets every Saturday. It also leaves exam-specific details as placeholders for the learner to fill in. A is easier to read on a fridge, but it reviews old units in blocks and leaves law and ethics out of weeks 1–2. It also relies on 'read and take notes' sessions and assumes the exam is the PTCE with a 60–70 minute practice-exam length. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers stay within the time budget and teach the three untouched units in Weeks 1–3. samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recommend B and explain that a multiple-choice test shows a rep can recognize a good answer, not give one. A handles the team lead's time better: it works out a concrete plan that cuts about 15 hours to about 5 (the lead runs one role-play per rep, peers run the other two, and the lead's sessions are in groups) and adds a scalable knowledge check for the VP. B's ideas are reasonable but vaguer. It never says how many hours the lead saves, and its fallback of two live rounds would still take about 10 hours of the lead's time. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend B and explain clearly that picking a multiple-choice answer shows recognition, not the ability to deliver a response live. B handles the time constraint better: it brings the lead's load from 15 hours to about 5 by having peers run two of the rounds, and suggests group sessions. B also gives the VP a concrete scalable piece, a 10-question pre-check on product and pricing facts. A's rubric and co-scoring ideas are good, but it never says how many hours it saves, it leaves a placeholder ('[current appointment-set or close rate]') in the text, and B's only weak spot is a fallback that cuts peer rounds, which doesn't free up any of the lead's time.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recommend B, explain that a multiple-choice test shows recognizing a good answer rather than giving one, calculate the 15 hours of team-lead time, and offer peer practice, recordings and a short auto-scored quiz to give the VP some scale. B edges ahead because it cuts the lead's time further (to about 4–5 hours) and makes the quiz scenario-based while saying plainly it is not proof of skill. It also adds a way to check later that the training worked. A's strengths are its concrete, Halvorsen-specific objections and its tighter writing, while B leaves a few placeholders unfilled. Neither answer cites made-up studies or statistics. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend B, separate recognizing a good answer from giving one, work out the 15 hours correctly and suggest peer practice, recordings and a short auto-scored check. B is a little stronger: it says plainly whether 15 hours is workable ('heavy but finite', spread over a week or two), and it uses real solar objections (rebates, roof, spouse) where A leaves placeholders like '[your top objections]'. Neither cites made-up studies or statistics.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recommend B, explain that a multiple-choice test only shows reps can recognize a good answer, cost B at about 15 hours of team-lead time, and propose trios or peer role-plays plus an auto-scored piece for the VP. A also offers recordings and a fallback if the lead has no time at all, but its '60–70%' time saving is stated as fact. B wins narrowly: it labels its 15→5–6 hour figure as an estimate, adds a later check to see whether the skill lasts, and points the VP to close rate instead of a test score. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend B, explain why a recognition test doesn't show live delivery, and work out that B costs about 15 lead-hours, with triads as the main way to cut that. B gives the VP more scale: recordings reviewed later, a separate auto-scored facts check, and a fallback if the lead has no time at all. A keeps scale through auto-scored scenario practice and adds a useful follow-up check. A labels its time-savings figures as estimates, while B states its 60–70% cut without that caveat, though the figure is plausible.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recommend B with peer pairs and keep a scaled check for the VP. A handles the team lead's constraint more concretely: it gives the correct ~15-hour figure, cuts the lead's time to about 5 hours, groups sessions to cut it further, and suggests asking the lead how many hours they can give. B pads its estimate to 20 hours, never says what the reduced load would be, and calls open-ended 'what do you say?' questions auto-gradable, which is doubtful, though tying the check to scenarios is a good idea. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend B and explain that a test shows a rep knows the right answer, not that they can say it live. A's plan for the lead's time is vaguer and contradicts itself: every rep gets a lead-observed session, yet the cost is described as only a first round plus a few drop-ins. pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recommend B, explain that multiple choice tests recognizing a good answer rather than giving one, run the 15-hour math correctly, and add a short auto-scored quiz to give the VP some scale. B's plan holds together better: two peer rounds, then one lead round, cuts the lead's time to about 5 hours, and it includes a fallback if even that is too much. A cuts the lead's time further, to about 75 minutes, but says everything fits in 2 hours when the demo plus three role-plays already takes about 105 minutes before prep, and its description of the peer rotation is muddled. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend B, explain that picking from options is different from giving an answer out loud, and add a short quiz to give the VP something that scales. A's math holds up: one lead round per rep is 15 × 20 minutes, or about 5 hours, and it gives a fallback if even that isn't possible. B says the lead can join one 20-minute round per rep, yet puts the cost at about 5 minutes per rep (75 minutes in total), which doesn't add up, and its description of how the peer role-plays rotate is muddled.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recommend B, explain that picking from a menu isn't the same as answering live, and offer peer role-plays and recordings to cut the lead's load. A's figure of about 19 hours isn't explained. A's fallback to a senior rep is useful, but its scale argument rests only on peer rubric scores. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend B with clear reasoning: a multiple-choice test shows reps can recognize a good answer, not give one out loud.
